findings.title: parallel::run with threads == 0 divides by zero in the generated C (SIGFPE), although the runtime documents threads <= 1 as harmless
findings.code_quote:
"/* Run [0,n) with `threads` workers in `chunk`-sized pieces; returns the first\n"
            " * non-zero worker result (0 = all fine). threads <= 1, or a thread that cannot be\n"
            " * created, is not an error: the range is simply finished on fewer workers. */\n"
...
            "    job.chunk = chunk > 0 ? chunk : (n / (threads * 8) > 0 ? n / (threads * 8) : 1);\n"
...
            "    if (n <= 0) return 0;\n"
            "    if (threads > 256) threads = 256;\n"
findings.why: The only call site of extc_par_run passes chunk = 0 literally (codegen.c:2317 emits `((int32_t)extc_par_run(__extc_par_%s, &%s, %s, %s, (int64_t)(%s), 0))`), so `chunk > 0` is false and `n / (threads * 8)` is evaluated with whatever thread count the extC program passed. threads == 0 makes that an integer division by zero, i.e. UB and SIGFPE in the generated program. Everything that would have made 0 harmless comes later: the `n <= 0` early return is after the division, the 256 cap is after it, and the worker loop `for (i = 1; i < threads; i++)` (which handles threads <= 1 correctly) is after it too. The runtime's own comment above the function promises `threads <= 1 ... is not an error: the range is simply finished on fewer workers`, so the code contradicts the contract it states; the checker accepts any i64 for `threads` (`parallel::run(worker, views..., n, threads)`), so nothing upstream rejects 0 either.
findings.trigger: Any program that calls `parallel::run(worker, <views>, n, threads)` with threads == 0 - e.g. a thread count computed from a config/argv value, or a count that came out 0 in a loop. n == 0 does not help: the division happens before the `n <= 0` return.

findings.title: extc_arena_alloc's size rounding overflows for n > INT64_MAX-7, returning a huge slice backed by a tiny block (wild writes)
findings.code_quote:
"static EXTC_MALLOC EXTC_NOINLINE void *extc_arena_alloc(extc_arena *a, int64_t n, const char *f, int l) {\n"
        "    if (n <= 0) n = 1;\n"
        "    n = (n + 7) & ~(int64_t)7;\n"
...
        "    if (!a->top || a->top->cap - a->top->used < n) {\n"
findings.why: `if (n <= 0) n = 1;` is the only sanity check on the requested byte count, and the alignment step `n + 7` is not guarded: for n in [INT64_MAX-6, INT64_MAX] the addition overflows (signed overflow, UB) and wraps to a negative value, which `& ~(int64_t)7` preserves. The block test `a->top->cap - a->top->used < n` is then false (a negative n is smaller than any free space), so no block is allocated and the caller receives `a->top->data + used` together with `used += n` (underflow). The caller builds a slice with `.len = n` (INT64_MAX), so every bounds check (`extc_checkedIndex`/`viewIndexer`) passes and the first store walks off the block. The intended behaviour for an unservable size is the trap already emitted at codegen.c:7352-7354 ("trap: out of arena memory (this allocation wanted %lld bytes)"), which the calloc-failure path produces; the overflow bypasses it. Note the sibling hazard at the call site: `new T[len]` is emitted as `(int64_t)(len) * (int64_t)sizeof(T)` with no overflow check, so for sizeof(T) > 1 the product wraps to a small/zero value even earlier (n >= 2^60 for i64) and the same wild-slice state is reached with an ordinary-looking length.
findings.trigger: A legal program that allocates with a byte size >= INT64_MAX-6, e.g. `new u8[n]` where n = 9223372036854775807 (a size taken from argv, a file header or an unchecked multiplication reaches this without the source ever writing the literal).
findings.repro:
cat > /tmp/t5.extc <<'EOF'
use std::io
fn main() -> i32 {
  let n: i64 = 9223372036854775807
  var p: mut slice<u8> = new u8[n]
  var i: i64 = 1000000
  let v: u8 = u8(65)
  p[i] = v
  i = i + 1
  io::cout << "read " << i32(p[i]) << "\n"
  return 0 }
EOF
./build/extc /tmp/t5.extc -o /tmp/t5.c && cc -std=c11 -O1 -fsanitize=address -o /tmp/t5a /tmp/t5.c && /tmp/t5a
# observed: ASan "SEGV on unknown address ... The signal is caused by a READ memory access" (the store/load is 1 MB past an ~88-byte block)
# expected: `trap: out of arena memory (this allocation wanted 9223372036854775807 bytes)` and exit 1

findings.title: f64 -> i64 conversion at exactly 2^63 is not trapped and is UB in the generated C ((double)INT64_MAX rounds up to 2^63)
findings.code_quote:
"static inline int64_t extc_convFloat(double v, int64_t lo, int64_t hi,"
        " const char *f, int l) {\n"
        "    if (!(v >= (double)lo && v <= (double)hi))"
        " extc_trapMsg(f, l, \"float does not fit in the target integer type\");\n"
        "    return (int64_t)v;   /* truncation toward zero, as in C */\n"
findings.why: The range test compares the double against the *converted* bounds. INT64_MAX is not representable as a double, so `(double)hi` rounds up to exactly 2^63 = 9223372036854775808.0; a value of exactly 2^63 therefore satisfies `v <= (double)hi` and reaches `return (int64_t)v;`, which converts a value outside the range of int64_t - undefined behaviour, and the promised trap ("float does not fit in the target integer type", the same promise the manually written sibling `extc_convFloatU` keeps by testing `v < 18446744073709551616.0`) never fires. i8/i16/i32 are unaffected only because their bounds are exactly representable; the emission site passes `INT64_MIN, INT64_MAX` for every 64-bit signed target (codegen.c:2605), so there is no narrower check to fall back on.
findings.trigger: An explicit conversion `i64(f)` where f is the double 2^63 exactly - e.g. the literal 9223372036854775807.0 (which rounds to 2^63 as a double), `9223372036854775808.0`, or any computation that lands on it.

findings.title: A payload-free generic enum instance is emitted as a tag+union struct while its values are bare enumerators, so the generated C does not compile (extc exits 0)
findings.why: The unit list is what decides which types get a C definition, and for enums it is filtered by payload: the non-generic loop above skips `!enumHasPayload(td)` (codegen.c:7687-7688) and a payload-free enum is emitted as a C enum typedef whose variants are enumerators (7620-7628). The instance loop has no such filter, and `unitBody`'s `if (u->td)` branch unconditionally emits `struct X { int tag; union { ... } u; }` (codegen.c:5225-5255), so `flag<i64>` becomes a struct type named `flag_i64` while the value emitted at the use site is the plain int enumerator `flag_i64_on` (the tag-constant block at 7892-7908 emits an anonymous `enum`, without a typedef). The result is an int value assigned to / compared with a struct type. `addInstanceUnit` (codegen.c:5459) carries the same missing payload filter, so the closure walk re-adds such a unit whenever a type mentions it.
findings.trigger: A generic enum with no payload on any variant, used as an instance: `type flag<T> = | off | on` then `let f: flag<i64> = flag<i64>::on`.
findings.repro:
cat > /tmp/t6.extc <<'EOF'
type flag<T> = | off | on
fn main() -> i32 {
  let f: flag<i64> = flag<i64>::on
  if f == flag<i64>::on { return 0 }
  return 1 }
EOF
./build/extc /tmp/t6.extc -o /tmp/t6.c ; echo $?   # observed: 0, no diagnostic; t6.c has `struct flag_i64 { int tag; union { } u; };` and `flag_i64 f = flag_i64_on;`
cc -std=c11 -O1 -o /tmp/t6 /tmp/t6.c               # observed: error: invalid initializer / invalid operands to binary == (have 'flag_i64' and 'int')
./build/extc /tmp/t6.extc --check-c -o /tmp/t6b.c  # observed: the same errors plus "extc: **the generated C does not compile** -- this is an extc bug"
# expected: the documented payload-free-enum shape (a C enum), as produced for a non-generic `type flag = | off | on`

findings.title: A coroutine declared as a method never gets its frame struct defined, so the generated C does not compile (extc exits 0)
findings.why: The synthesized coroutine frame is a plain C struct whose definition comes from `unitBody` (`cType` renders the type as `struct %s$frame`, codegen.c:483-486), and a unit is created only for coroutines found in `m->funcs` (this loop) or in `g.funcs` with a template (the loop at 7717-7725, for generic instances). A coroutine *method* lives in `sd->methods`, is therefore absent from `m->funcs`, is pushed into `g.funcs` by 6989-6999 and has its `$step` body emitted by the body loop at 8227-8237 - but no unit is ever created for its frame type, so the C names `struct box_run$frame` without defining it. Free-function coroutines work, so the gap is exactly the method case.
findings.trigger: A coroutine written as a method and driven as a frame: `struct box { v: i64 }`, `impl box { fn run(self: ref box, n: i64) -> coroutine<i64> { ... yield ... } }`, `var fr = b.run(i64(2))`, `while fr.next() {...}`.

findings.title: The parallel region is sized and initialized with the uncapped thread count; counts >= 2^60 wrap the size computation into a heap-buffer-overflow
findings.why: `extc_par_run` opens the region with the caller's raw count (`extc_par_open(threads > 0 ? threads : 1)`, codegen.c:8410) and only afterwards clamps the worker count to 256 (codegen.c:8415), so the clamp cannot bound the allocation. For workers >= 2^60 the product `(size_t)workers * sizeof(extc_arena)` is 0 modulo 2^64, calloc returns a 16-byte block, `r->workers` is set to the huge count and the initialization loop writes 16 bytes per iteration past the end of that block immediately - heap corruption from a legal program. (A moderately huge count is no better: the region is allocated and initialized for the full count, 16 bytes per entry, while at most 256 workers are ever created.) The doc block above the function says an unusable thread count is "not an error", so silently corrupting memory is not the intended fallback either.
findings.trigger: `parallel::run(worker, views..., n, threads)` with a large threads value (>= 2^60 for the overflow; a much smaller but still huge value for unbounded allocation) *and* a worker that allocates (the checker sets usesHome, which is what makes the region half compile in and pass withRegion = 1).

findings.title: The "the compiler needs this name" guard skips array and enum instances, so a user declaration with that name produces two C definitions of one struct (extc exits 0)
findings.why: This loop is the guard that rejects a user declaration whose name the compiler needs for a generated instance, and it gives a precise diagnostic for generic struct instances. Its filter requires `inst->kind == TY_GENERIC && inst->sdef`, which excludes exactly the two other kinds of instance that also produce a C struct under a generated name: array instances (`ttArray`, types.c:130-141, `sdef == NULL`, name `array_<n>_<elem>`) and generic enum instances (`ttEnumGeneric`, types.c:701-715, kind TY_ENUM). For those the guard never fires, and the instance unit emits a second definition under the same tag, so the C compiler reports a redefinition inside generated code - the failure mode this check exists to prevent ("the error points into the generated C, where the user cannot see their own source", cSymName's own rationale).
findings.trigger: `struct array_2_i64 { x: i64 }` together with any `[2]i64` value, or `struct maybe_i64 { x: i64 }` together with any `maybe<i64>` value (the names are documented by the diagnostic the guard does print for struct instances: `<type>_<argument>`).

findings.title: markUncalledFunctions lacks the dynTable exemption its sibling pruner has, so a method the dyn table calls is marked EXTC_UNUSED
findings.why: The decision is "the name occurs exactly in its own declaration and definition, so nothing calls it". For a method that a `dyn` table dispatches to, that premise is false: the vt thunks are only appended at the very end of generateC (`bufPuts(out, bufCstr(&vtDefs))`, codegen.c:8575), long after this pass runs, so the only mentions in the text at this moment are the prototype and the definition and the method is attributed `EXTC_UNUSED`. The sibling pruner in `dropUnreferenced` already knows the answer is not available yet and carries the exemption: `if (df->dynTable) continue;   /* named by a `dyn` table, which is spliced in later */` (codegen.c:6341; the flag is set from the checker's `f->dynTable`, check_expr.c:665, through `deadFuncBody`). The attribute is therefore a false statement about a called function - precisely the warning class the pass was written to avoid (its own comment: "putting it on one that *is* called is wrong (`-Wused-but-marked-unused` reports exactly those, one per call site)").
findings.trigger: A `dyn` dispatch through a trait implemented for a generic type, where the method has no other mention in the program: `trait Tag { fn tag(self: ref Self) -> i64 }`, `struct pair<T> { a: T }`, `impl<T> Tag for pair<T> { fn tag(self: ref pair<T>) -> i64 { return i64(1) } }`, `dyn Tag(p).tag()`.

coverage_notes: Read src/codegen.c:6451-8578 in full (four chunks), plus the helpers it depends on that live just above the range (identByte/countSpan/countPut/countGet at 5587-6299, dropUnreferenced at 6301-6425, ensureUnusedMacro at 6434-6456) and the cross-file definitions of the invariants I relied on (types.c ttArray/ttMangle/ttEnumGeneric, check_expr.c:630-670 for dynTable/used, check.c:455 for coroBoxed, docs/reviews/engineering-review-1.md for which earlier findings are already fixed). Verified as correct rather than reported: funcDefStart's column-zero-'}' end scan and its p != at guard (6490 vs the fixed F17); markUncalledFunctions/markUnusedParams offset arithmetic (insertions applied from the end backwards, buffer replaced through bufCstr, so no offset is invalidated) - the O(n^2) copy per insertion is real but the marked set is small and I could not make it matter; the '`own == count`' test cannot wrongly mark a function that is called from text already present, and the `$`-aware identByte (5592) makes the countSpan tokenizer correct for `io$name` symbol names, which I had suspected as a hole; the recursion-depth guard (extc_rec_enter at 7141 plus cgRecLeave at 3076/3111 and the fall-off path at 4945) decrements on every exit including the implicit one; extc_print/extc_eq match tools/print-formats.txt byte for byte (struct `name {  }`, `[a, b]`, bare variant names, %g, text slice<u8>); the vtDecls/vtDefs split does declare the table before the bodies and the thunks before the table definition; the arena spare/release/destroy and lazy-zero logic is otherwise sound (the only hole is the n+7 overflow reported above); the descriptor/SCALAR_DESC rows cover exactly the eleven builtins plus ref/text; cSymName's pointer-identity test at 6744 is valid for keyword/operator renames; emitDescRegion restores g->out before genCoroHandleDecls. Two smaller observations not filed as findings: `CG.coroDefs` (204, 6978, 8574) is appended to the unit but never written to by any code, so the comment at 8571-8573 ('coroutine frames and step functions: appended here, after every byte-offset pass') describes a mechanism that does not exist - the frames come from the units list and the $step definitions from the ordinary body loop; and clang -Wused-but-marked-unused also fires on the hardcoded EXTC_UNUSED declarations of extc_coro_next/extc_coro_value_* (4498/4513/4538), which is the same warning class as the dynTable finding but outside this range. Not reproduced, only reasoned about: none.
